storylines.label: Attack Security
storylines.latest_title: Did the attack work? Auditing AI-agent security benchmark verdicts

editorial.tldr: This is a loose research thread on agent security, not one event. It opened with an arXiv paper arguing that coding harnesses wired to shells, filesystems, and sockets become Living-off-the-Land platforms once an injected instruction lands.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 19 audit questions whether AI-agent security benchmarks score attacks correctly, asking if reported "attack succeeded" verdicts actually hold up.
editorial.why_it_matters: If benchmark verdicts on agent attacks are unreliable, the security scores you use to pick a harness or guardrail may not reflect real exposure.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before trusting an agent-security benchmark score, spot-check a sample of its "attack succeeded" and "attack failed" verdicts against the raw transcripts.

storylines.label: Routing Inference
storylines.latest_title: How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

editorial.tldr: This is a loose topical cluster, not one event: four independent items that each use "routing" to cut inference cost, latency or capacity risk at a different layer. OpenRouter rebuilt provider routing on Oct 30, a Show HN introduced the Sibyl local appliance on Nov 7, and the C²-Routing paper applied routing to VLM inputs on Nov 10.
editorial.whats_new: AWS describes how Salesforce uses the SageMaker AI cross-Region inference router (Nov 18) to pool fragmented Regional capacity, adding capacity across Regions and accounts for reliable model serving.
editorial.why_it_matters: "Routing" now names four separate levers (which provider serves a request, which local backend runs it, how much input reaches the model, and which Region has capacity), and each is tuned, evaluated and failed over differently.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as four independent decisions. If you serve on SageMaker AI and hit Regional capacity limits, check cross-Region routing against your data-residency rules and measure the added latency; re-measure OpenRouter traffic after its routing rebuild.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures

editorial.tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Oct 30 it ran through pruning, Anthropic's Nov 2 provable-inference update, knowledge editing and eval-validity work to Nov 13-16 papers on when a model should abstain, ask or escalate.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 18: a contrastive-prototype method detects jailbreak prompts without training a separate guard model, after Nov 16-17 papers on calibrated abstention thresholds and provenance-aware decoding for omnimodal hallucinations.
editorial.why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but the recent run converges on guardrail design: calibrated refusal, modality-aware hallucination control and lightweight jailbreak screening, each a component a serving stack can test.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before swapping in any of these guardrails, replay your own traffic: measure the jailbreak detector's false-block rate on benign prompts, check that a calibrated abstention threshold holds its error rate on your data, and count the extra model calls each method adds.

storylines.label: Multi-Agent Systems
storylines.latest_title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems

editorial.tldr: This is a loose research cluster, not one event: early November papers covered RL theory, orchestration benchmarks, and KV-cache memory for co-resident agents. From Nov 4 the work tilted toward securing multi-agent systems and attributing their failures, from NIST identity tenets to CoLFA and AgentLeak.
editorial.whats_new: Two new papers push from diagnosis to repair: TRACE-MAS (Nov 17) diagnoses and repairs collaboration failures between agents, and Kaer (Nov 18) adds security-aware replanning to orchestrators that revise plans mid-run.
editorial.why_it_matters: The open problems in multi-agent stacks are now securing, debugging, and paying for them: agent identity, data leakage, which agent caused a failure, how to repair it, and KV-cache memory per resident agent.
editorial.take_for_builders: Log which agent produced each message and plan revision, and scope each agent's credentials, so you can attribute failures and leaks; treat the repair and replanning papers as research until code is released and replicated.

storylines.label: Scientific Discovery
storylines.latest_title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents

editorial.tldr: This is a research thread, not one event: three arXiv papers on LLM agents that run scientific discovery. SciMARS (Nov 9) adapts multi-agent harnesses for closed-loop experiments, and Contrastive Discovery (Nov 10) argues agents should test competing explanations instead of one hypothesis against its negation.
editorial.whats_new: Openhagen Worlds (Nov 18) adds calibrated environments meant to measure whether a discovery agent picks informative experiments, separate from recall, hidden scoring rules or shortcut policies.
editorial.why_it_matters: Discovery-agent claims are hard to trust until an eval can separate experiment choice from memorized answers, and Openhagen Worlds is the first paper in this thread aimed at that gap.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you build research or data-analysis agents, borrow the eval idea first: test experiment choice in environments where recall cannot reveal the answer, and treat benchmark gains without such controls as unproven.

storylines.label: Recursive Self-Improvement
storylines.latest_title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement

editorial.tldr: September's recursive self-improvement (RSI) papers retrained models on their own output; November's wave instead has agents rewrite their harness (prompts, tools, memory, control loop) with the base model frozen. Early November added a benchmark for that loop, a statistical-guarantee method to keep it trustworthy, and a multi-agent version for closed-loop science.
editorial.whats_new: Two Nov 18 papers push RSI back into the weights: BaseRSI internalizes harness gains into a base vision-language model without training, and Piccolo co-evolves 0.8B-27B decision models with their own training data.
editorial.why_it_matters: Harness-level RSI means an agent can change its own prompts, tools, and memory in production, so the harness itself becomes a versioned artifact that needs evals and rollback.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent edits its own prompts, tools, or memory, version every self-edit and gate it on a held-out eval with a rollback path before it reaches production.

storylines.label: Continual Learning
storylines.latest_title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge

editorial.tldr: October's papers framed continual learning around forgetting, replay selection and agent benchmarks. November turned to cheaper adapters: RASP (Nov 2) keeps a single fixed-size LoRA instead of one branch per session, and a Nov 9 paper shares one prompt across tasks with no rehearsal data.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 18: two papers move continual learning toward deployment, one adding specialist vision models to a trained multimodal agent's tool space, the other (Hypnos) running continual learning end to end on edge devices.
editorial.why_it_matters: Updating a deployed model or agent without retraining or regressions is the cost problem here; fixed-size adapters and incremental tool addition are the mechanisms that would make it cheap.
editorial.take_for_builders: Do not adopt yet; if you add tools or fine-tune adapters on a live agent, rerun the old task evals after each update to catch regressions.

status.detail: Four arXiv papers in November; all research-stage, none shipped in a product or framework.

editorial.tldr: This is a loose thread of unrelated model technical reports, not one developing event. It opened with Tencent Hunyuan's Hy-Nomas world-model report and benchmark on Oct 30, then MNN-Pocket-0.3B, a 300M-parameter on-device model with 32K context, on Nov 9.
editorial.whats_new: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview's report (Nov 18) describes a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35B total and 3B active parameters that supports a thinking mode.
editorial.why_it_matters: Each report shows a different serving shape: world models, sub-1B INT4 on-device models, and sparse diffusion LMs, each with its own inference cost and runtime needs.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as research reads. Before adopting one, check its weight license and runtime support, especially for Clover's diffusion decoding.

storylines.label: Knowledge Context
storylines.latest_title: NaviGATE: Noise-Aware Dual-View Generation for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Reasoning

editorial.tldr: This is a loose cluster of mostly arXiv papers on agent training, alignment and knowledge handling, not one developing story. It started with RL recipes, preference-optimization variants and kernel-tuning agents, then widened to retrieval, agent memory and vision-language grounding work.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 18: NaviGATE proposes noise-aware reasoning over multimodal knowledge graphs, after a week where Jetriever ranked agent memories by usefulness instead of similarity and PhysScope targeted physics-diagram agents.
editorial.why_it_matters: If you run RAG or agent memory, these papers name concrete failure modes (models answering from pretraining instead of retrieved context, similarity search returning unhelpful memories, stale personal facts), but every result is author-reported on the papers' own benchmarks.
editorial.take_for_builders: Add eval cases where the retrieved context or image contradicts the model's prior (altered facts, decoy diagrams) and check the agent follows the evidence before adopting any new retrieval, memory or alignment recipe from this cluster.

storylines.label: Weight-Space Programming
storylines.latest_title: Can Weight-Space Programming Alter Learned Ethical Priorities?

editorial.tldr: On Nov 3, Latent Space covered an MIT result showing frontier LLMs can read and write small neural network weights directly, with no training run. Over the next two weeks an open-source instruction set, a game-agent compilation paper, and an independent replication followed.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 18 arXiv paper tests whether a weight edit can change a model's ethical trade-off, raising the benefit needed to override a formal pledge in a concept-supervised text model.
editorial.why_it_matters: If LLMs can author and inspect weights directly, model behavior becomes editable without a training run, which is both a new tooling surface and a new tampering risk for anything you serve.
editorial.take_for_builders: Hold off on production use: results so far cover small networks and research models. Do add checkpoint hashing and behavior regression evals, since direct weight edits leave no training trail.

storylines.label: Cost Inference
storylines.latest_title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades

editorial.tldr: This is a loose research thread on inference cost, not one event. It opened with an arXiv paper arguing that per-token billing hides cost: each token added to the KV-cache makes later tokens more expensive, so energy grows non-linearly with sequence length.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 18 arXiv paper proposes timeout cascades to cut the GPU cost of coding agents, two days after an open-source benchmark compared OSS inference vendors on cost and latency.
editorial.why_it_matters: Long-context and agentic workloads cost more than flat per-token prices suggest, so vendor choice and agent run limits are cost levers, not just latency settings.
editorial.take_for_builders: Measure your agent's cost per completed task across context lengths before picking a vendor, and test a timeout cap on long-running agent attempts.

storylines.label: Speculative Decoding
storylines.latest_title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers

editorial.tldr: Speculative decoding research in late summer split between new drafters (diffusion draft trees) and context-heavy agent workloads (AsymSpec). Early November papers then went after the drafter itself: per-token reconsideration, block-diffusion fork trees, phrase-level drafting, and two losses that train directly for acceptance length.
editorial.whats_new: Callo (Nov 13) and LoopCache (Nov 18) move the thread to serving: Callo starts decoding agent requests whose KV cache was invalidated before re-prefill finishes, and LoopCache adapts self-speculation to looped Transformers' per-loop caches.
editorial.why_it_matters: For agent serving, the gap now named in papers is not draft quality alone but long or edited context, where KV-cache invalidation and re-prefill stall decoding under prefill-decode disaggregation.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agents edit context mid-session, measure re-prefill stall time on cache-miss requests before tuning drafters; drafter-level gains from these papers stay paper-only until they land in your serving stack.
